Warehouse Shift Handover and Inventory Guide
This guide sets out how shift supervisors at our distribution sites conduct handover and keep
inventory records consistent between crews. It covers the handover sequence, counting duties,
discrepancy escalation and the records that must survive each transition. Every procedure here
applies across the 4 operating sites and is reviewed on a 12-month cycle. Supervisors should
treat the written handover as the single authoritative record of what one shift passes to the next.
1 Handover Principles and Shift Boundaries
Handover is a controlled transfer of responsibility, not a conversation. The outgoing supervisor
remains accountable until the incoming supervisor signs the handover sheet, and the incoming
supervisor assumes custody of keys, seals and open tasks at that moment. Boundaries are fixed
by roster, and no shift may close without a countersigned sheet. Where a boundary is disputed,
the site manager decides and records the decision.
Supporting records are presented in Table 1.
1.1 Preparing Before the Boundary
Table 1: Shift boundary responsibilities by role
Preparation begins well before the boundary. The outgoing supervisor confirms that pick queues
are cleared or explicitly carried forward, that damaged goods are segregated, and that the dock
area is secured. Preparation checklists are completed in sequence so that nothing is signed off
prematurely. Any task that cannot be finished is written as a carry-forward item with a named
owner and a realistic completion window.
1.1.1 The Handover Walk and Verbal Briefing
The walk follows a fixed route through receiving, storage, packing and dispatch so that both
supervisors see the same conditions. The briefing then covers open orders, safety observations,
equipment faults and staffing gaps. Neither the walk nor the briefing replaces the written sheet.
Supervisors should keep the walk brisk but complete, pausing only where a physical condition
needs to be shown rather than described.
Supporting records are presented in Table 2.

Table 2: Handover walk checkpoints and what each confirms
1.1.1.1 Confirming Physical and System Status
Physical status and system status are confirmed separately, then reconciled. The outgoing
supervisor demonstrates that seals are intact, that quarantine cages are locked and that scanner
devices are docked and charging. The incoming supervisor checks the warehouse management
system for open tasks and confirms that the system view matches what was seen on the walk.
Differences are noted before either supervisor signs.
1.1.1.1.1 Seals, Keys and Equipment Custody
Custody of seals, keys and powered equipment transfers only against a signature. Each item is
listed with its identifier and condition, and any missing item is escalated immediately rather than
noted for later. Equipment with a reported fault is tagged out and removed from the available
pool. The incoming supervisor confirms that chargers, batteries and access cards are accounted
for before releasing the outgoing crew.
1.1.1.1.2 Open Orders and Carry-Forward Tasks
Open orders are listed with order reference, priority and the reason they remain open.
Carry-forward tasks are limited to those that genuinely cannot be completed within the outgoing
shift, and each carries an owner and a deadline. The incoming supervisor may re-prioritise but
must record the change. Tasks carried forward repeatedly across shifts should be raised to the
site manager as a capacity signal.
1.1.1.2 Handover Sheet Completion and Signatures
The handover sheet is completed in full before either supervisor leaves the floor. It records the
boundary time, the walk findings, open orders, equipment condition and any escalations raised.
Both supervisors sign and time-stamp the sheet, and the incoming supervisor files it in the shift
log. Incomplete sheets are not accepted; a supervisor who cannot complete the sheet must
escalate to the site manager before departing.
Supporting records are presented in Figure 1.

1.1.2 Escalation During Handover
Some conditions cannot wait for the next routine review. Safety hazards, suspected theft, failed
seals and system outages are escalated to the site manager during handover, not after it. The
escalation is recorded with the time raised and the response received. Where the site manager is
unreachable, the duty manager acts, and the attempt and outcome are both written on the
sheet.
1.2 Handover Records and Retention
Completed handover sheets are retained in the shift log for audit and dispute resolution. Records
are stored so that any past shift can be reconstructed from the sheet, the system log and the
equipment register. Retention periods are set by site policy and reviewed with the cycle.
Supervisors should treat the log as evidence, writing entries that a reader unfamiliar with the
shift could follow without asking questions.
2 Inventory Counting and Reconciliation
Inventory accuracy depends on disciplined counting and honest reconciliation. Counts are
scheduled by zone and product class, and each count is performed by someone other than the
person who last handled the stock where staffing allows. Results are compared with system
balances, and every variance is investigated before an adjustment is posted. The guide treats
counting as a control activity, not a clerical chore.
Supporting records are presented in Figure 2.
Figure 2: Count method by zone type
2.1 Count Scheduling and Method
Counts are scheduled so that high-velocity zones are checked more often than slow-moving
storage. Counters use the approved method for each zone, whether full count, spot check or
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT | RESEARCH PROTOTYPE
cycle count, and record the method used. Blind counts are preferred so that counters are not
anchored by expected figures. The schedule is published in advance and adjusted only with the
site manager's agreement.
2.1.1 Recording Count Results
Count results are recorded at the point of counting, not reconstructed afterwards. Each entry
shows the location, product reference, quantity observed and the counter's identifier. Corrections
are made by annotation rather than overwriting, so the original observation remains visible. The
incoming supervisor reviews recorded results during handover and flags any zone where
counting was interrupted or left incomplete.
2.1.1.1 Variance Investigation and Adjustment
A variance is investigated before any adjustment is posted. The investigator checks recent
movements, misplacements, unrecorded returns and possible scanning errors, and documents
which explanations were tested. Adjustments require approval from a supervisor who did not
perform the count. Where the cause cannot be established, the variance is recorded as
unexplained and monitored across subsequent counts rather than written off silently.
2.1.1.1.1 Locating Misplaced Stock
Misplaced stock is the most common explanation for a variance and should be sought before any
adjustment. The investigator searches adjacent locations, overflow areas and the quarantine
cage, and checks whether a put-away was scanned to the wrong bin. Findings are recorded with
the location where stock was actually found. Repeated misplacements in one zone point to
labelling or layout problems rather than individual error.
2.1.1.1.2 Approval and Posting of Adjustments
Adjustment approval is separated from counting and from stock handling. The approver reviews
the investigation record, confirms that plausible explanations were tested, and either approves,
queries or rejects the adjustment. Approved adjustments are posted promptly so that system
balances reflect reality before the next shift. Rejected adjustments return to the investigator with
a written reason, and the stock remains flagged until resolved.
Supporting records are presented in Table 3.
Table 3: Adjustment approval decision criteria
2.1.1.2 Cycle Count Sampling and Coverage
Cycle counting samples a rotating portion of locations so that every zone is covered within the
review cycle. Sampling is planned rather than opportunistic, and coverage is tracked so that
neglected zones become visible. A sample of 240 location checks per cycle is the planning
SYNTHETIC DOCUMENT | RESEARCH PROTOTYPE
reference for coverage across the 4 sites. Counters should not select their own samples, and
coverage gaps are reported at handover.
2.1.2 Discrepancy Escalation and Fraud Indicators
Most discrepancies are errors, but some patterns warrant escalation. Repeated shortfalls in one
product class, missing seals, or stock found outside recorded locations without explanation are
referred to the site manager. The guide does not treat these patterns as proof of wrongdoing;
they are indicators that require a documented review. Escalation records distinguish observed
facts from inferences drawn from them.
2.2 Improving Handover and Count Accuracy
Accuracy improves through small, sustained changes rather than periodic campaigns.
Supervisors should review handover sheets and count variances together to spot recurring
causes, such as unclear labelling or rushed boundaries. Suggestions are logged and reviewed at
the cycle review, and adopted changes are briefed at handover. Progress is judged by fewer
repeat variances and cleaner handover sheets, not by a single good week.
